presentingComplaint: Increasing confusion and reduced oral intake for 1 day, on a background of 2 days of loose stools and vomiting
history: 84-year-old frail nursing-home resident (Clinical Frailty Scale 6, baseline mild dementia) brought in by carers because she became more drowsy and 'not herself' overnight. Over the preceding 48 hours she had 6-8 episodes/day of watery, non-bloody, non-mucoid diarrhoea and several episodes of vomiting, with progressively poor oral intake. Two other residents on her floor developed a similar short self-limiting diarrhoeal illness in the past week (suspected facility outbreak). No dysentery, no tenesmus, no recent travel. No antibiotic or PPI exposure in the last 90 days. Comorbidities: hypertension, mild CKD (baseline creatinine ~1.0 mg/dL), dementia. In the elderly the illness has presented atypically - dominated by delirium and volume depletion rather than by GI symptoms, which the family under-reported.
examination: Frail, drowsy but rousable, disoriented to time and place (delirium; GCS 14). Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3-4 s - clinically dehydrated. Abdomen soft with mild generalised discomfort, no guarding, no rebound, no focal peritonism; bowel sounds active. No rash, no meningism, chest clear, no CVA tenderness, no suprapubic tenderness.

labs.comment: Pre-renal AKI (creatinine risen from baseline ~1.0), hypernatraemic dehydration and hypokalaemia from GI losses; mild leucocytosis and CRP rise

imaging: Erect chest and supine abdominal X-ray unremarkable - no free air, no obstruction, non-distended gas pattern. (Imaging performed to exclude an intra-abdominal mimic given the atypical delirium presentation.)
microbiology: Blood cultures sent. Stool sent for culture, ova/parasites and C. difficile GDH/toxin - C. difficile toxin negative. Stool multiplex viral panel positive for norovirus (facility outbreak); no invasive bacterial pathogen isolated. Urinalysis negative for nitrites/leucocytes.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute infectious gastroenteritis (norovirus outbreak) with dehydration and pre-renal AKI
Invasive bacterial diarrhoea (dysentery) - argued against by absence of blood/mucus/tenesmus
Clostridioides difficile infection - argued against by no antibiotic/PPI exposure and negative toxin
Sepsis of alternative source (e.g. UTI) presenting as delirium in the elderly
C. difficile / drug or metabolic delirium
finalDiagnosis: Acute infectious (viral) gastroenteritis in a frail elderly patient, complicated by hypovolaemic delirium, hypernatraemic dehydration and pre-renal acute kidney injury
citations: IDSA - Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea - 2017
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
ICMR - Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes (Acute Gastroenteritis) - 2022
stewardship: Mainstay of management is aggressive fluid and electrolyte resuscitation (isotonic IV rehydration with cautious sodium correction and potassium replacement), not antibiotics - most acute gastroenteritis, including this norovirus outbreak, is self-limiting and antimicrobials are not indicated. Empiric antibacterial therapy is reserved for the subset with severe febrile illness, sepsis or dysentery; given this frail elderly patient's fever, tachycardia, hypotension and borderline lactate, an empiric course was started at presentation before stool results returned and de-escalated/stopped once norovirus was confirmed and C. difficile excluded. When empiric therapy is chosen, azithromycin (WHO AWaRe Watch) is the guideline-concordant agent (covers Campylobacter/Shigella, avoids fluoroquinolone toxicity in the elderly). Avoid antimotility agents in possible invasive disease.
contraindications: Avoid loperamide/antimotility agents if invasive/inflammatory diarrhoea is suspected
Avoid empiric fluoroquinolones in the frail elderly (QT, tendinopathy, delirium, C. difficile risk)
Correct hypernatraemia slowly (<10 mmol/L/24h) to avoid cerebral oedema
Nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast) contraindicated with pre-renal AKI
edgeCases: In the elderly, gastroenteritis frequently presents as delirium, falls or dehydration with under-reported GI symptoms
Facility outbreak clustering strongly suggests norovirus and argues against a bacterial cause
Negative C. difficile toxin with no antibiotic/PPI exposure makes CDI unlikely despite institutional residence
Hypovolaemic pre-renal AKI can be mistaken for intrinsic renal failure if the volume history is missed
expectedMaiK: Recognise acute infectious gastroenteritis with hypovolaemic delirium and pre-renal AKI in a frail elderly patient; prioritise IV rehydration and electrolyte correction, send stool/blood studies, and treat supportively rather than reflexively with antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: Stool character - any blood, mucus or tenesmus (to distinguish invasive dysentery)?
Any antibiotic, PPI or hospitalisation exposure in the last 90 days (C. difficile risk)?
Baseline renal function and usual fluid/oral intake and medication list (diuretics, ACE-i, nephrotoxins)?
Urinary and respiratory symptoms to exclude an alternative sepsis source causing delirium?
expectedInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine (assess dehydration, hypernatraemia, hypokalaemia, AKI)
Venous lactate and CRP; full blood count
Stool culture, ova & parasites, and C. difficile GDH/toxin
Stool multiplex/viral PCR (norovirus) in the outbreak setting
Blood cultures and urinalysis to exclude an alternative sepsis source

investigations: Stool culture, ova/parasites and C. difficile toxin

regressionAssertions: Must recommend fluid/electrolyte resuscitation as primary management
Must flag pre-renal AKI and hypernatraemic dehydration secondary to GI losses
Must not misclassify as DYSENTERY given absence of bloody stool/tenesmus
Must consider and appropriately exclude C_DIFF (negative toxin, no antibiotic/PPI exposure)
Empiric antibiotics (azithromycin) reserved for severe febrile presentation and stopped once norovirus confirmed
Must avoid antimotility agents and fluoroquinolones in this frail elderly patient
